Across five benchmarks, PreView improves the average grounding accuracy of Qwen3-VL-2B, OS-Atlas-4B, and Qwen3-VL-4B without further training these grounding models. Extensive analyses examine the contributions of views and cues, center refinement, and visual input budgets.

all_scored.title: DROA-CLIPSeg: Prompt-Guided Thin Crack Segmentation in Low-Light Conditions
all_scored.summary: Pavement crack segmentation under low light is degraded by reduced contrast, shadows, headlight glare, joints, stains, and wet seams. Existing crack segmentation methods mostly assume good illumination. Low-light enhancement methods improve visual quality, but they do not explicitly preserve crack topology. To address these limitations, we formulate low-light crack segmentation as a degradation-aware, prompt-grounded structural defect segmentation problem and propose DROA-CLIPSeg, a parameter-efficient framework that adapts a frozen CLIPSeg vision language backbone using two lightweight modules. QKV Low-Rank Adaptation is injected into the Q/K/V projections of the vision and text encoders to improve crack-specific image text alignment without backbone fine-tuning. The proposed Domain Residual Orthogonal Adapter (DROA) decomposes intermediate features into a dominant crack-domain branch, which captures recurring low-light crack patterns, and an orthogonal residual branch, which preserves faint, thin, and fragmented evidence usually suppressed by noise, shadow, or over-smoothing. We also introduce CrackLingo-9K and CrackLingo-12K, text augmented versions of Crack9k and Crack12k with crack-aware prompts. Training only approximately 1.93 M parameters, corresponding to 1.3% of the full model, DROA-CLIPSeg outperforms 9 zero-shot and 4 fine-tuned vision language baselines on both splits, generalises zero-shot to MVTec AD across textures and defect morphologies, and is supported by extensive ablations. Our source code is publicly available at https://github.com/VShuklacode/DROA-CLIPSeg

all_scored.title: ProbeID: Verifying MCP Tool Identity for LLM Agents under Registry Drift
all_scored.summary: Agents select tools by copyable descriptions, which cannot establish which implementation runs. ProbeID compares canonicalized responses to schema-valid probes with a trusted admission reference and abstains on ambiguity, so a squatter must copy probe-observable behavior. With the gold present, independent probes and a fixed margin, standard concentration arguments give a shared probe budget logarithmic in the candidate count and bound the joint probability of a wrong decision. On cached MCP-IdentityDrift cases, strict choice reaches \(0.956\) hit@1 while description routers fall near chance, but simpler exact comparisons tie it, MMD better tolerates heavy value noise, and a 32B behavioral judge is similarly accurate at higher cost. Random probes from agent banks and a prospective held-out study of 38 tools test theory-set thresholds. On the agent banks, equality refuses every reachable replacement from 64 probes and the bounded distance from 512, and sharper post hoc gates halve both. Two tools whose drift no bank probe reaches always pass. In an MCP-Bench agent, verification cuts tainted tasks from 15 to 9 of 16 at unchanged task success. Over eleven weeks, 7 of 59 real tools changed responses despite version pins. Verification depends on reference integrity, probe coverage, and response noise.

all_scored.title: A Model-Theoretic Formalization of AlKhwaremis ilm alfaraid
all_scored.summary: This paper presents a model theoretic and computational formalization of AlKhwarizmis treatment of inheritance within the framework of Computational Fiqh. We first show that every inheritance configuration in a specified class is representable as a finite system of rational linear equalities and inequalities, and that such systems are decided exactly by Fourier Motzkin elimination over Q. We then define the fixed dimensional inheritance structure Vd with distinguished claimant coordinates, and prove that every admissible rational linear coordinate realization is isomorphic to Vd, this establishes the algebraic representation as canonical within that class. The complete first order theory Td of Vd is shown to be complete by construction and is explicitly distinguished from the decidability of the inheritance relevant fragment. The methodological principle is then related to a broader formalization of closed Fiqh domains via exhaustive case generation, Horn clause axiomatization, and terminating deduction, yielding domain relative computational completeness.

all_scored.title: Graph-dependent pooling: adaptive granularity in hierarchical graph neural networks
all_scored.summary: Graph Neural Networks are widely used to learn structural representations of relational data. Hierarchical graph pooling learns multi-level representations by progressively coarsening graphs; however, prior methods rely on predefined cluster numbers or fixed pooling ratios, limiting adaptability to individual graphs. We propose Graph-Dependent Pooling (GDPool), which dynamically determines pooling granularity for each graph. We analyze optimization conflicts among layer-wise objectives through gradient alignment, showing that independently supervised pooling levels can send conflicting gradients to shared parameters. GDPool uses self-attention to select graph-specific anchors representing structurally important nodes and constructs coarse graphs through soft node assignment. Experiments on metal-organic framework and molecular graph benchmarks show that GDPool consistently achieves the best predictive performance across all benchmarks. Evaluations using modularity and the effective number of clusters show that GDPool achieves consistently higher modularity than existing methods while the number of active clusters decreases monotonically with depth. Sensitivity analyses confirm stable behavior across hyperparameter and architectural choices.

all_scored.title: Geodesic-SVDD Latent Mixup for One-Shot Distributed Tabular Learning
all_scored.summary: Distributed Learning on structured data is a key and widely adopted approach in privacy-sensitive sectors, ranging from financial fraud prevention to federated healthcare diagnostics. While Gradient Boosted Decision Trees are widely used in centralized settings due to their efficiency, they are incompatible with standard gradient-based federated learning protocols because of their non-differentiability. Conversely, standard deep classifiers that are amenable to federated optimization often suffer from catastrophic forgetting under label distribution skew. In this work, to address these gaps we propose Geodesic-SVDD, a framework for Distributed Spherical Prototype Learning that recasts each client's task as one-class density estimation on the hypersphere, so that local models can be aggregated as probabilistic manifolds in a single round. Specifically, for each client, we employ a Residual Spherical Encoder and Geodesic Latent Mixup that enforces strict hyperspherical constraints ($\|φ(x)\| \equiv 1$), preventing the manifold collapse observed in linear approximations. Furthermore, leveraging this insight, we propose a novel One-Shot "Product of Experts" protocol that enables privacy-preserving aggregation without iterative synchronization. Finally, we mechanistically analyze the trade-off between interpolation strategies, demonstrating that while linear mixup offers an enticing computational shortcut, it destabilizes optimization gradients by orders of magnitude ($10^9\times$). Across five tabular benchmarks and four levels of label skew, Geodesic-SVDD attains the highest mean AUROC among seven federated methods, outperforms federated tree ensembles by up to 21 AUROC points on Covertype, and its One-Shot variant matches centralized Deep SVDD under IID and mild skew with a single communication round.

all_scored.title: On the Error Analysis of Triangular Transport Maps for Conditional Generation via MMD-based Objectives
all_scored.summary: Conditional generative models parameterized by triangular transport maps are widely used for conditional sampling, yet theoretical guarantees on the quality of the conditional measures they produce remain scarce. We address this question for minimum divergence estimators of triangular maps. We use MMD-based objectives as a tractable setting in which the gap between joint and conditional errors can be analyzed precisely, and we measure performance through the average conditional estimation error, defined as the squared maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) between the estimated and the true conditionals, averaged over the conditioning variable. We first show that the common practice of minimizing a joint MMD may fail to recover the conditionals: writing the joint and the conditional criteria as quadratic energies of the same conditional mean embedding residual, we prove that, for parametric classes, joint minimizers are generically inconsistent in the misspecified setting. We then analyze an estimator that directly minimizes the conditional criterion through a surrogate loss computable from joint target samples and reference samples. We prove a non-asymptotic error bound that decomposes the average conditional estimation error into approximation, estimation, and reference sampling errors, with fast rates independent of the ambient dimension in the parametric setting. Finally, for joint MMDs built from concentrating Gaussian kernels on the conditioning variable, we show that the joint criterion approximates a density-reweighted version of the conditional one, and we derive an error bound for the joint minimizer whose rate suffers from a curse of dimensionality in the conditioning variable. Our results suggest that training criteria for conditional generative models should target the conditional rather than the joint error, a principle that extends to other divergences and to dynamic transport.

all_scored.title: H-GLow: Accelerating Graph Generation via Hazard-Guided Discrete Flow Matching
all_scored.summary: Discrete flow matching (DFM) offers a promising approach to graph generation; however, generating high-quality graphs with few steps remains challenging due to the strong dependencies between nodes and edges. Although DFM decouples training from sampling, enabling flexible sampling strategies without retraining, existing graph DFM samplers often rely on task-specific heuristics, substantially expanding the hyperparameter space. Moreover, graph DFM models still require sampling budgets comparable to those of diffusion-based approaches, leaving their potential for accelerating graph generation only partially realized. In this work, we introduce H-Glow, a hazard-guided framework for accelerating graph generation built on the decomposition of Continuous-Time Markov chain (CTMC) generators into hazards and conditional jump distributions. H-Glow leverages these quantities to plan graph edits and dynamically adjust the sampling time to graph activity. H-Glow can be adapted to pretrained graph DFM models, substantially improving the generation quality with fewer steps. We further introduce a novel graph DFM model based on the conditional generator matching framework, which directly predicts hazards and conditional jumps, and show that its training objective decomposes exactly into hazard matching and hazard-weighted jump prediction. Experiments on molecular and synthetic graph benchmarks demonstrate improved generation quality with substantially fewer sampling steps.

all_scored.title: Counterfactual Model Testing Under Distribution Shift
all_scored.summary: Deployed machine learning (ML) models can degrade as the distribution of their input data shifts. Such shifts can result from changes in the population or from data integrity issues in the pipeline that materializes model features, two sources that operate through different mechanisms. Because labels are often absent or delayed, it is common practice to track shifts in the data instead, but a detected shift does not indicate how it affects the model. We formulate this problem as online model testing under distribution shift. Testing requires reproducing the shift on a controlled baseline with known labels. Since the same shift can come from either source, doing so requires knowing which mechanism changed. We propose a methodology that reproduces observed changes in both mechanisms to estimate current performance and the potential gain from repairing observed data integrity issues. Experiments on real-world datasets with simulated faults show that separating the two sources generally improves both estimates, supporting this formulation. A churn prediction case illustrates how these tests can support monitoring and repair prioritization

all_scored.title: Variational Atlas Autoencoders and Self-Supervised Chart Selection
all_scored.summary: Complex, high-dimensional data lie on manifolds that a single global latent coordinate system cannot represent without distortion. We introduce Variational Atlas Autoencoders, a mixture-of-charts framework that learns an atlas of local latent representations, each responsible for one region of the data manifold. The central difficulty in learning an atlas is deciding which chart should be responsible for which data point without labels. We show that this decision need not be a heuristic. By treating the chart index as a latent variable, the evidence lower bound yields the training objective and casts chart assignment as posterior inference, valid for any routing distribution. Within this framework, we propose latent-evidence routing, which assigns a point to a chart in proportion to the evidence of its encoding under that chart's latent prior. This has a simple interpretation: the closer a point lands to the center of a chart's latent space, and the more confidently it is placed there, the more likely it is to belong to that chart. Chart assignment thus emerges as posterior inference, depends on the encoder alone, and is fully self-supervised, so the charts discover structure in the data on their own, separating classes and subclasses such as distinct types of shoes or faces without access to labels. We further recover an atlas from the trained charts by identifying their overlaps and transition maps, enabling continuous interpolation within and across charts that stays close to the data manifold rather than traversing unsupported regions of latent space. Compared to capacity-matched baselines, Variational Atlas Autoencoders yields better-structured latent spaces and higher sample quality on image datasets including CelebA, while sampling requires evaluating only a single chart's decoder.

all_scored.title: Hybrid-time PINNs: Discontinuity-Aware Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Learning Hybrid Dynamical Systems
all_scored.summary: Hybrid dynamical systems flow continuously but jump at discrete events. Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) fit data while enforcing known dynamics, but a single network is smooth in time and cannot model these jumps. We show that the more closely a PINN follows a jump, the larger its physics loss must be. We propose hybrid-time PINNs (HT-PINNs), which assign one network to each flow interval of the hybrid time domain and train the networks jointly with the jump times and the unknown parameters. The number of jumps and the sequence of modes are found by enumeration. HT-PINNs recover the number of jumps and the restitution coefficient of a bouncing ball. In a MuJoCo simulation of robotic disassembly, where a robot pulls a press-fitted pin out of a housing through a spring, HT-PINNs find the number of jumps and the sequence of modes, and estimate the static and kinetic friction coefficients with small errors of 0.1% and 1.7%.

all_scored.title: Joint End-to-End Training of Weighted BP Decoder Ensembles
all_scored.summary: Ensemble decoding improves decoding reliability by combining component decoders with complementary failure events. Existing approaches typically obtain this diversity from code-specific structure, such as code automorphisms, multiple parity-check representations, or targeted modifications of the message-passing graph. In this work, we instead learn the diversity of an ensemble of weighted belief propagation decoders by jointly optimizing trainable Tanner-graph edge weights. A central design question is how the training objective should distribute gradient among the ensemble members to promote complementary decoding behavior. To this end, we compare four ensemble objectives under direct gradient-based optimization and identify best-member training as the most effective approach. For a (64,32) progressive edge-growth (PEG) low-density parity-check (LDPC) code, the resulting ensemble outperforms the considered trained and untrained belief-propagation-based ensemble baselines. With 10 members, it provides a gain of approximately 0.66 dB over a single belief propagation decoder at a target frame error rate (FER) of $10^{-4}$. Similar behavior is observed for a (128,64) CCSDS LDPC code, indicating that the learned complementarity is not specific to PEG. Although the ensemble performance improves substantially, all trained members show a higher standalone FER. The gain therefore results from learned specialization and complementary failure events rather than uniformly improved component decoders.

all_scored.title: SEDATE: Do Large Language Models Share an Aggression Circuit Across Languages?
all_scored.summary: As the applications of AI continue to expand across various multimodal and multilingual domains, ensuring safe and responsible deployment of these systems has become an important concern. A wide-range of interventions have been proposed to make AI responses safer and more reliable. They often incur substantial computational or annotation costs, or cannot be extended to multilingual settings. In this work, we propose Selective Detection And Targeted Editing (SEDATE), a training-free approach based on detect-edit-verify strategy. SEDATE first detects the responsible neurons, edits them as and when necessary and finally verifies the model responses; all without any additional model training. We evaluate SEDATE across 7 languages and 4 model families. We further evaluate its effectiveness across 4 out-of-distribution languages and 4 additional datasets. We show that SEDATE achieves substantially superior safety scores across all languages and models over the best-performing baseline while retaining the general capabilities and incurring negligible overhead. Our results are robust, with the trends remaining similar for out-of-distribution languages and datasets.

all_scored.title: Patch-Derived or Register Tokens? Comparing Variable-Length Image Tokenizers
all_scored.summary: Image tokenizers convert pixels into compact latent sequences for efficient generative modeling. Most approaches arrange latents on a downsampled two-dimensional grid, tying sequence length to image resolution. We compare two variable-length strategies: computationally efficient patch-derived tokens, which inherit explicit spatial organization, and more demanding register tokens, which have no predefined spatial layout. Our reconstruction results reveal that patch-derived tokens perform substantially better under extreme compression, whereas register tokens achieve slightly better reconstruction quality at intermediate budgets. At high token budgets, both approaches achieve similar reconstruction quality. For downstream generative tasks, register tokens outperform patch-derived tokens. Adding representation alignment with external pretrained visual encoders substantially improves the generative performance of patch-derived tokens, allowing them to match or outperform register tokens depending on the token budget. We further find that both approaches learn spatially localized representations. Patch-derived tokens largely retain their explicitly imposed spatial organization, while register tokens develop an implicit two-dimensional spatial structure despite having no predefined layout. Representation alignment reduces this spatial organizational constraint, enabling individual tokens to exert a stronger non-local influence.

all_scored.title: Clustering of High-Dimensional Human Gene Score Data for Target Cell Classification
all_scored.summary: The goal is to investigate whether the total human gene-score dataset and the selected human kinase-gene dataset exhibit the same number of clusters when analysed using the same set of 769 features. Two datasets were considered: the complete gene score dataset and a subset containing selected kinase genes. Two missing-data strategies were investigated. In Case I, rows containing missing gene-score values were removed. In Case II, rows with more than 20% missing values were excluded and the other missing values were replaced by the corresponding column mean. For each case, the data were scaled and principal component analysis (PCA) was performed before clustering. Four clustering approaches were considered: K-Means, Hierarchical Clustering, Fuzzy C-Means, and Graph-based Clustering. Across both datasets and both missing-data treatments, the optimal number of clusters was found to be two. In the absence of an optimal number of clusters, the quality of clustering was assessed using the Silhouette score. Relatively high Silhouette scores were obtained in all cases.

all_scored.title: Pacifo: An Efficient Fully Homomorphic Encryption-based Lightweight ResNet for Trustworthy Machine Learning as a Service
all_scored.summary: Machine Learning as a Service (MLaaS) has become a popular paradigm for deploying AI applications. However, it raises significant privacy concerns that the raw client data needs to be uploaded to the server for inference services. Private inference using Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) offers a solution by allowing computations directly on encrypted data, with only the final results decrypted on a client side. However, current practical implementations still suffer from large computational overhead and high latency due to the cost of FHE operations. In this paper, we propose Pacifo, a framework that adapts customized fine-tuning strategies to efficiently evaluate the ResNet20 model in the context of FHE. Specifically, Pacifo introduces a public-private layer partitioning scheme and an efficient ReLU approximation, significantly reducing the number of private layers and costly FHE operations during inference. It also offers flexible security configurations to accommodate varying client privacy requirements. Compared to state-of-the-art FHE implementations of ResNet20, Pacifo achieves a speedup of $3.7-21.7\times$ in runtime while effectively preserving $95\%-99\%$ of the original plaintext model accuracy across downstream tasks. Pacifo is open-sourced at https://github.com/BryceYangLi/Pacifo.

all_scored.title: Optimizing Physical Neural Networks through Device Variable Selection
all_scored.summary: Physical neural networks (PNNs) leverage device physics in electronics, optics, and related domains to enable energy-efficient neural networks. Broken-isomorphism PNNs replace linear operations with multivariate physical transformations, modifying how input signals are mapped to device variables. We exploit network architectures emerging from these mappings by treating the routing between signals and input variables of physical devices as trainable parameters. This approach expands device-level tunability of the physical transformations while, at the system level, demonstrating improved expressivity of PNNs with negligible additional inference overhead. This discrete routing is optimized by training a categorical distribution using Gumbel-Softmax reparametrization. We evaluate this approach using experimentally calibrated differentiable models of multivariate electronic RNPUs for MNIST and CIFAR-10 classification. Using variable selection, we improve the MNIST classification accuracy for a small CNN model from 94.5% to 96.9% and the accuracy of CIFAR-10 from 62.8% to 68.0%. Our method uniquely leverages the induced biases of broken-isomorphism PNN architectures, paving the way towards more efficient physics-based neural network inference.

all_scored.title: One Model, Two Paths: Balancing Single-Pass and Looped Performance in Language Models
all_scored.summary: Repeating Transformer layers can improve language-model performance without adding parameters. A pretrained model can be adapted to support both single-pass and looped inference by reusing middle-layer weights for additional computation. Because both paths share weights, training to improve looped predictions can degrade single-pass quality. We study joint training strategies using weighted losses on both outputs, with guidance from the frozen original model. Joint supervision substantially reduces single-pass degradation compared to looped-only training, while preserving looped gains over ordinary continued training. Most of this benefit comes from adjusting the single-pass loss weight, with guidance from the frozen original model further improving the looped output. With validation-selected weights, our method preserves single-pass quality within a predefined tolerance of ordinary continued training while improving looped predictions.

all_scored.title: Affine-invariant Cubic Newton with Weak Learners
all_scored.summary: Modern gradient boosting algorithms are based on Newton's method, which excels empirically but lacks global convergence guarantees. While recent work on Gradient-Regularized Newton (GRN) boosting achieved a global $\mathcal{O}(1/γ^{12}k^2)$ rate, its analysis was not able to exploit the natural Hessian geometry and suffers from a heavy $γ^{12}$ dependence on a worst-case `weak gradient edge' $γ$. In this paper, we tackle these theoretical drawbacks by generalizing the Affine-Invariant Cubic Newton (AICN) scheme to convex optimization with weak learners. Our analysis is based on average cosine values $\overlineΘ_k$ along the optimization path and directional improvements $δ_k$ in the Hessian-induced norm. We show that the weak-AICN update reduces to a damped weak-Newton step with an explicit stepsize determined by $δ_k$. Under semi-strong self-concordance, we establish a global $\mathcal{O}(1/\overlineΘ_k^4 k^2)$ rate, significantly improving upon the weak-GRN bound. We further prove a local linear rate, global linear convergence for Hessian-dominated losses, cosine angle lower bounds, and present weak-AdaAICN, which adaptively tunes the cubic regularization. Finally, we demonstrate the broader applicability of this framework beyond gradient boosting by showing that Newton coordinate descent emerges naturally as a special case of optimization with weak learners.

all_scored.title: Collective Collaboration of Recursive Autonomous Agents
all_scored.summary: Smart factories must translate order-level objectives into production tasks at multiple scales and combine the capabilities of individual units into an overall delivery capability. To address repeated adaptation of organizational mechanisms across equipment, workshops, and factories, as well as coordination across levels under changing production conditions, this paper develops a framework for the collective collaboration of recursive autonomous agents (RAAs). A common task and capability interface supports the recursive decomposition of production objectives from the top down and the aggregation of conditional capabilities through peer collaboration from the bottom up. Composite units can therefore participate in higher-level organizations as agents of the same kind. We formulate organizational models for leaf and composite units, specify interface closure under composition and conditions for finite task expansion, and develop operational mechanisms linking task decomposition, resource commitments, result aggregation, and coordination within the scope affected by change. A production network integrating machining, inspection, and logistics across multiple workshops illustrates how a common organizational kernel is instantiated at the equipment-service, workshop, and factory scales. The framework connects recursive organization with explicit task responsibilities, capability conditions, and execution interfaces for manufacturing systems.

all_scored.title: Overlap-Aware Sub-hypergraph Pattern Frequencies for Hypergraph-Level Classification
all_scored.summary: Classifying whole hypergraphs requires a fixed-length description of inputs whose numbers of vertices and hyperedges vary. Frequent sub-hypergraph patterns provide such a description, but previous work records only whether each pattern is present, which loses two kinds of information: how large the overlap between two hyperedges is, and how much of a hypergraph each pattern makes up. We extend frequent sub-hypergraph mining with overlap labels, the binned intersection size of two pattern hyperedges inherited from the target hypergraph, and represent each hypergraph by the relative frequency of each mined pattern. The vocabulary is mined from training hypergraphs only and then frozen, and validation and test hypergraphs are matched against it. A support rule that depends on pattern size keeps the vocabulary small. On the six hypergraph-classification datasets of DHG-Bench, with a single configuration chosen on validation scores, the method has a higher mean Macro-F1 than the best published mean on five datasets, by 18.67 points on Twitter-Friend and 10.02 points on Steam-Player; on RHG-3 it is 0.21 points lower. Ablations show that on Steam-Player and Twitter-Friend, replacing relative frequencies with presence lowers Macro-F1 by about 18 points, and that removing overlap labels lowers it by 4 to 9 points.

all_scored.title: FedSEAM: Federated Continual Learning of LLMs via Subspace Expert Agreement Merging
all_scored.summary: Federated continual learning trains a model on a sequence of tasks across several clients without sharing their data while retaining knowledge of earlier tasks. Sparse mixture-of-experts models support this setting by adapting selected parameters on a frozen backbone. However, clients learn different expert content as tasks evolve, making it difficult to share knowledge across clients without disrupting task-specific and client-specific specialization. Matching tile coordinates alone does not establish whether their learned content is compatible. We present FedSEAM, a federated continual learning framework that organizes task knowledge into sparse experts and selectively shares their content across tasks and clients. On each client, task-aware tile selection allocates capacity to a new task, while a subspace-based compatibility test determines which existing expert tiles to reuse and where to introduce fresh capacity. On the server, Subspace Expert Agreement Merging (SEAM) compares client updates as subspaces and moves each client towards consensus only along agreed-upon directions, leaving the rest of its update unchanged. We identify two remaining sources of forgetting, routing drift and merge erasure, and address them with three protections, one of which exactly preserves tile components in a selected prior-overlap subspace at every merge. We evaluate FedSEAM on TRACE using Qwen3-4B and Llama-3.2-3B, with component-wise ablations and studies of data size to assess its balance between learning new tasks and retaining prior knowledge.

all_scored.title: Five Architectures, One Shared Space Cross-Model Representational Alignment Without Weight Merging
all_scored.summary: Combining language models is usually done by averaging weights, which works only when the models share a common starting point. We ask whether five frozen, independently trained models with different internal designs (four transformers from four organizations and one state-space model) can be related through their activations alone, with no weight merging. Using permutation tests, an independent replication probe set, depth sweeps, pooling ablations and confound checks, we find statistically robust correspondence between how the five models organize the same text. It is strongest at each model's final layer and weaker for the state-space model, whose weakest pairing is still 35-43 times chance. We use this to build a shared space with Generalized Procrustes Analysis, in which no model is a fixed reference. At the final layer, mean held-out retrieval accuracy over the twenty ordered model pairs is 0.91 to 0.93 on two probe sets (chance 0.03), beating pairwise linear maps (0.82 to 0.85), but the space is worse than those maps in the middle layers. It transfers to ordinary English of unfamiliar grammatical form and fails on mathematical and logical notation. We then test whether the space supports a router that picks among the five models on gradeable tasks. Across four task types we find no case where routing beats always using the strongest model, and we report this as a negative result. A correctness signal that looked strong turned out to be category membership in disguise. All experiments ran on one laptop without a GPU.

all_scored.title: Explicit Frictional Contact Modeling in Neural Garment Simulation
all_scored.summary: Graph neural networks (GNNs) simulate garments efficiently through physics-based self-supervision, but leave body-garment friction implicit or inside training energies, with no friction coefficient $μ$ to set at inference; retraining the tested GNNs with a coefficient-specific friction term barely responds to $μ$. Optimization-based solvers decide each contact's stick-slip state from the reaction that governs it, but only by re-optimizing the garment state at every step; a friction term in a one-pass training objective acts as a fixed-weight penalty on sliding, and the trained weights apply no per-contact Coulomb condition at inference. We therefore resolve friction explicitly after prediction: a Modular Contact Operator, attached to a frozen predictor without retraining or an iterative solve, estimates the normal load, applies a closed-form Coulomb correction along a path across body triangles, and propagates the induced motion through the cloth as a linearized membrane wave. On HOOD and ContourCraft, it raises sticking and lowers slip monotonically in $μ$, tracking a reference solver's response while coefficient-specific retraining stays flat, with low penetration and reference-consistent stretching at an eighth of the solver's runtime.

all_scored.title: Error-Subspace Calibration for Multi-Task Model Merging
all_scored.summary: Model merging combines task-specific expert models into a single model without joint training on their original datasets, but often incurs a performance gap relative to the individual experts. Post-merging calibration can reduce this gap through task-specific representation alignment, but the alignment objective alone does not specify which feature directions to correct. We propose Error-Subspace Calibration (ESCal), a post-merging calibration framework that identifies low-dimensional error subspaces from weight differences between expert and merged models. At each intermediate block boundary, a bridge module projects the merged representation onto the next block's input-projection error subspace and maps these coordinates to an additive correction in the current block's output-projection error subspace. The subspace bases remain fixed, so calibration learns only these linear maps, yielding a parameter-efficient mechanism for feature correction. We find that ESCal brings the merged model closer to the experts in both representations and predictions, indicating more faithful recovery of task-specific behavior. Experiments on vision and natural language understanding benchmarks show that ESCal improves merged-model performance across diverse architectures and merging methods using a small calibration set for each task.

all_scored.title: Climate downscaling with likelihood functional flow matching
all_scored.summary: Decisions about heat, frost and flooding are made locally, yet reanalyses and climate models resolve tens of kilometres. Generative downscalers add kilometre-scale detail with uncertainty, but are tied to a grid, costly to sample and lack a tractable likelihood. Here we introduce CD-FFM, a functional flow-matching model that treats the high-resolution field as a continuous random field that one model can query at any location and resolution. Its velocity acts pointwise, so spatial variability comes from a noise prior fitted to the observed spectrum and every observation has an exact likelihood. Downscaling ERA5 to 1 km daily temperature over Fennoscandia, CD-FFM lowers the continuous ranked probability score by 27-31% against regression and 12-18% against a forty-times larger neural operator in each of three test years, and outperforms a CorrDiff-style diffusion model while sampling about fifty times faster. The same model transfers to precipitation and makes large kilometre-scale ensembles affordable.

all_scored.title: A Differentiable Chassis Safety Layer for Intelligent Vehicle Motion Control
all_scored.summary: Learning-based vehicle motion control requires coordination between diverse task objectives and state-dependent chassis safety constraints. Conventional cascaded architectures may compromise task performance when safety filters modify nominal commands independently of policy learning. This article proposes a differentiable chassis safety layer that modularly integrates task-oriented control with explicit physical constraints. Actuator limits, individual-tire force constraints, and vehicle handling envelopes are incorporated into sequential quadratic programs. Each projected command propagates the predicted vehicle dynamics and updates subsequent constraints, enabling temporal gradient coupling through implicit differentiation. A two-stage learning strategy combines expert imitation with risk-guided supervision and conditional intervention guidance to coordinate nominal control decisions with chassis safety constraints. Closed-loop evaluations under unseen scenarios, emergency maneuvers, and ablation studies demonstrate that the proposed method improves safety-performance coordination and exploits vehicle dynamic potential while maintaining handling stability.

all_scored.title: SCET-CBF: Speed-Calibrated Soft Guidance for One-Step Dynamic Navigation
all_scored.summary: Control barrier functions (CBFs) support collision avoidance, yet dense dynamic encounters can leave a vehicle with no feasible command. Geometric refinements and soft constraints help preserve motion choices. Using these choices also requires accounting for the vehicle's changing turning response. For a steering-limited bicycle, braking can lower closing speed while slowing the lateral motion needed before an obstacle arrives. We propose SCET-CBF, a speed-calibrated soft guidance law for one-step dynamic navigation. A short lateral escape maneuver gives an allowable approach speed. Its speed derivative allows a quadratic program to weigh both effects of braking when choosing acceleration and steering. Soft penalties accommodate competing obstacle preferences within the input set permitted by segment and braking constraints. We derive the guidance and establish protection over each accepted motion segment, together with conditional braking invariance for a single obstacle. On 2500 paired tasks with a 60 s deadline, SCET achieves 72.8% completion, compared with 49.8% for CBF/velocity-obstacle control and 69.8% for an enhanced 1 s CBF-MPC. At 100 obstacles, SCET and the enhanced MPC complete 52.4% and 33.6% of tasks. Paired studies identify the contributions of speed feedback and early activation. Further evaluations examine the operating range under lateral acceleration limits and bounded motion and execution errors.

all_scored.title: The Future Is Finer: Multivariate Time Series Super-Resolution Forecasting
all_scored.summary: Web platforms run on multivariate time series, from service telemetry and Web traffic logs to sensor streams served through Web APIs. Yet, retention policies often archive them at coarse granularity to save storage and bandwidth. Decisions such as autoscaling, alerting, and billing operate at finer granularity than existing forecasters reach, since these models predict at the resolution of their input. We therefore introduce Multivariate Time Series Super-Resolution Forecasting (MTS-SRF), which forecasts fine-grained futures from coarse histories, and propose TimeMagnifier to address its three challenges. Fourier Anchor counters data sparsity by fitting each input window to a trend-Fourier structure with sparse cross-variable gating; De-noise Only constrains fine-grained ambiguity by refining along the resolution axis rather than the noise axis, lengthening the grid level by level; and banded DTW Alignment corrects cross-resolution misalignment against the coarse forecast. On the first MTS-SRF benchmark, with ten datasets from five domains, real archived cross-resolution pairs, strengthened baseline adaptations, and five-seed significance tests, TimeMagnifier is best on every dataset, resolution coefficient, and metric against 15 baselines and cuts MSE by 12.3% on average. Its De-noise Only and DTW stages also transfer as a plug-in that lowers the MSE of existing forecasters by 5.1% to 9.0%. Code will be made publicly available.

all_scored.title: Propasafe-Hybrid: A Text-Based Hybrid Propaganda Detection Tool
all_scored.summary: Propagandistic content increasingly circulates through online news and social media, where readers often encounter it with limited scrutiny, highlighting the need for reliable and fine-grained detection. This paper introduces Propasafe-Hybrid, a sentence-level system that integrates a fine-tuned transformer classifier with LLM-based technique classification to identify, label, and explain specific propaganda strategies. The pipeline generates actionable outputs, including highlighted sentences, technique assignments, and concise rationales, so users can immediately understand why a sentence was flagged and how each label was determined. To control inference cost, Propasafe-Hybrid employs a cost-aware pre-filtering stage that forwards only high-likelihood sentences to LLMs, reducing token usage while preserving the underlying decision logic. Together, these design choices enhance the explainability, efficiency, and practical usability of sentence-level propaganda detection in real-world news environments.

all_scored.title: FG-ConvNO: A Geometry-Aware Neural Operator for Propeller CFD Prediction
all_scored.summary: Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) is essential in contemporary engineering design, yet it remains expensive to compute and can take thousands of CPU/GPU hours or more for a single high-fidelity simulation. Recent developments in machine learning for scientific modeling have led to powerful surrogate frameworks that can approximate flow fields and physical quantities by using a fraction of the computational cost. However, most of these methods require largescale homogeneous datasets or simple geometries, exhibiting severe generalization gaps when applied to complex and data-scarce configurations. To address this, we propose the Factorized Geometry Convolutional Neural Operator (FG-ConvNO) for robust geometry-aware propeller pressure prediction under limited training data. We introduce geometryaware encoding, efficient interpolation-based decoding, and auxiliary global quantity supervision. In addition, we incorporate DISCO blocks that use discrete continuous convolutions to make the model discretization agnostic. In our experiments, FG-ConvNO achieves the highest accuracy for both surface pressure and global thrust prediction on a procedurally generated propeller CFD dataset. Geometry-aware encoding and architectural simplification improve stability, while random vertex subsampling enhances robustness. Overall, adding geometric priors to grid-based convolutional operators reduces overfitting on complex propeller geometries and improves generalization in low-data regimes.

all_scored.title: Examining form-based linguistic productivity in people and large language models
all_scored.summary: Linguistic productivity, as evidenced by the use of words in novel contexts, is one of the most striking facts about human language. However, how abstract the knowledge that enables such productivity is remains unclear. We compare people's and computational language models' linguistic productivity in contexts where successful generalization depends on form-based information. We focus on extending the use of a novel verb learned in the active voice to passive contexts. We find people extend active to passive uses in a way consistent with abstract generalizations concerning linguistic form, even when no plausible meaning can be assigned to the novel verb. In contrast, large language models succeeded only when a meaning like an existing verb's could be assigned to the novel verb. We conclude that computational models' syntactic knowledge remains tied to the distribution and meaning of specific lexical items in a way that human syntactic knowledge is not.

all_scored.title: Exact Unlearning After Data Curation
all_scored.summary: Training pipelines often remove similar examples before fitting a model. Deleting a raw record can change that selection and admit an example that was excluded before. What must a service retain to reproduce training after such requests? We answer this question for a fixed rule in which earlier similar records block later ones. A limit on the total number of future deletions identifies exactly which records can still enter training. We use this boundary to build a summary of training statistics that can be repaired exactly after repeated deletions. The repaired summary is the same as rebuilding it on the surviving data with the remaining budget. We also construct finite-precision features for ridge regression, a linear learner with a penalty on coefficient size. With exact rational outputs, allowing one more deletion changes the required private information. It rises from zero to every private feature sign in the excluded candidates. An encoding attains this conditional private-information minimum on the constructed family throughout a sequence of requests. On 1,001 AskUbuntu development records, deleting an initially excluded record admits another record at 13 of 51 fixed similarity cutoffs. Exact membership repair passes 13,056 deletion-step checks. Two model-based semantic calibrations fail their fixed criteria, so the downstream task study is not run. The central result is a retention contract: the future deletions a service promises to support determine which excluded data can still be needed.

all_scored.title: Online Covariance Estimation for Averaged Stochastic Gradient Descent on Riemannian Manifolds
all_scored.summary: We study online inference for averaged Riemannian stochastic gradient descent (RSGD) when the unknown parameter lies on a manifold. Although the averaged RSGD iterate is asymptotically normal, practical inference requires estimating the unknown covariance operator in its limiting distribution. Existing online batch-means methods cannot be applied directly because a general Riemannian manifold lacks an addition operation, and the tangent space containing the Riemannian gradient varies across iterations. Through vector transport, we construct overlapping and non-overlapping covariance estimators that adaptively combine information from successive batches while accounting for the changing tangent spaces. The proposed estimators are online, require neither Riemannian Hessian computations nor a prespecified terminal sample size, and attain the same convergence rates as their Euclidean counterparts (Zhu et al., 2023). Together with asymptotic normality, these estimators enable online statistical inference for RSGD on manifolds. We illustrate the proposed framework through a detailed study of streaming principal component analysis on Grassmann manifolds.

all_scored.title: Agent-to-Agent Synthetic Social Engineering on the Web
all_scored.summary: An AI agent can prepare an accurate report and still request an action its user has not authorized. Cooperation across Web services therefore requires separate judgments about identity, evidentiary support, and permission. We define synthetic social engineering (SSE) as deliberately deceptive or misleading influence intended to exploit AI recipients' responses to credibility, authority, or obligation cues and redirect behavior away from authorized objectives. We focus on separately tasked sender agents that produce or adapt misleading communication. Drawing on cybersecurity, social engineering, and persuasion research, we develop an operational framework connecting actors, deceptive representations, candidate influence routes, evidence or permission boundaries, responses, and consequences. The framework distinguishes attempts from successful redirection, without assuming human psychological processes. We implement it in the Agent Service Exchange and Evidence Commons (ASE-EC), a reproducible testbed with independently specified records and authorization scopes. Across 1,260 research episodes using Qwen3-4B in two fictional briefing tasks, matched comparisons test authority and commitment appeals, while defense comparisons assess protection alongside authorized task completion. Invoking a limited prior agreement increased unauthorized requests from 43.3% to 96.7%, although recipients retained supported decisions and permissions remained unchanged. These controlled findings identify action selection as a distinct security concern, even when evidence handling succeeds, and they provide a reusable basis for evaluating safeguards that preserve useful cooperation across Web services.

all_scored.title: Faithful Federated Tabular Data Synthesis
all_scored.summary: Synthetic data is an important data source in the AI era. This paper studies the generation of mixed-type tabular synthetic data in federated settings, where two key challenges arise: ensuring distributional fidelity and effectively handling mixed-type data. We propose Federated Integrative Two-Step Synthesis (FITS), a framework for mixed-type tabular data synthesis. At its core is a two-step federated algorithm for estimating conditional cumulative distribution functions (CDFs) using local linear regression. Building on this algorithm, we develop a federated synthesis procedure based on the probability chain rule to ensure distributional fidelity. To handle mixed-type data, FITS introduces a continualization method that lifts discrete variables into a continuous space and recovers their discrete distributions without loss at both the density-function and CDF levels. This transformation provides a unified continuous representation of mixed-type variables, facilitating the application of local linear regression and synthetic data generation. Our theoretical analysis characterizes the conditional density and cumulative distribution functions of the continualized mixed-type variables and establishes the uniform convergence of the resulting federated conditional CDF estimators. Experiments demonstrate that FITS-generated synthetic data improves downstream task performance for all clients, with the benefits depending on how the synthetic data is used.

all_scored.title: The Cost of an Unknown Horizon for the Last Iterate of Clipped SGD under Heavy-Tailed Noise
all_scored.summary: Training is often stopped at a data-dependent time, as in early stopping, and the last iterate is kept. Guarantees valid at such times must hold at all times simultaneously. We determine the optimal time-uniform rate for the last iterate of clipped SGD on smooth convex objectives under heavy-tailed noise with a bounded central $p$th moment, $1<p\le2$. A schedule without horizon or confidence inputs attains $\tilde O(t^{-β_p})$ at all times, with $β_p=2(p-1)/(3p-1)$, also almost surely, and no rule that steps along the stochastic gradient at its current iterate attains $\tilde O(t^{-r})$ for any $r>β_p$, even with adaptive step sizes and thresholds. This rate lies between the optimal rate $O(T^{-α_p})$ for a known horizon $T$, $α_p=(p-1)/p$, and the previous time-uniform rate $\tilde O(t^{-2(p-1)/(3p)})$ (Chezhegov et al., ICLR 2026); under finite variance, the exponents are $1/2$, $2/5$, and $1/3$. Their conjecture that a better schedule reaches the optimal rate thus holds with a known horizon, as shown by Liu and by Jiang et al., but fails without one. Querying gradients at the running average of the iterates attains $\tilde O(t^{-α_p})$ at all times, whereas heavy-ball momentum with geometric forgetting and polynomially bounded steps cannot improve on $β_p$.

all_scored.title: One Call Ahead: Packed Self-Speculative Decoding with Diffusion Drafting
all_scored.summary: Autoregressive (AR) language models generate tokens sequentially, so generating long outputs is costly. Speculative decoding mitigates this by using a lightweight drafter to propose multiple tokens for the target AR model to verify in parallel, while a diffusion-based drafter can produce an entire draft block in one forward pass. In models with AR and diffusion modes, one network both drafts and verifies, but drafting still waits for verification, so the standard schedule needs two sequential model calls per iteration. Existing one-call schedules avoid the wait but incur input size quadratic in the speculative width. Motivated by this efficiency bottleneck, we introduce Packed-SS, a self-speculative decoding schedule that verifies and drafts in a single model call with input size linear in the speculative width, while preserving the target model's distribution. The key idea is to let the diffusion drafter run one call ahead: while verifying the current draft, the model simultaneously constructs the next draft from an older verified prefix and keeps its unresolved suffix for the next iteration. Under a mild monotonicity assumption on the drafter, we further show that Packed-SS requires no more model calls than the standard two-call decoding in the greedy setting. Experiments on Nemotron 3B/8B and SetDLM 1.7B show higher throughput and lower mean wall time than both baselines under greedy decoding.

all_scored.title: Automated screening of Parkinson's Disease using Smooth Pursuit Eye Movements
all_scored.summary: Smooth pursuit eye movements are frequently altered in Parkinson's disease, but previous studies have relied mainly on conventional parameters that describe the relationship between gaze and target. This study investigates whether complexity and nonlinear dynamics measures of the gaze position sequences can support the automatic screening of Parkinson's disease. Gaze position sequences were recorded with a video eye tracker in 41 participants with early Parkinson's disease and 47 healthy controls during 12 smooth pursuit tasks. Four experimental frameworks and four embedding delay strategies were compared. The selected experimental setting combined baseline wander removal with a fixed embedding delay. After feature selection, a support vector machine was trained for each task and axis and their outputs were combined in a mixture of experts. The pipeline was developed in 70 participants and evaluated on an external test set of 18 participants. On the external test set, the pipeline obtained an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.86. The most informative features described less persistent and more irregular gaze position sequences in Parkinson's disease, mainly along the horizontal axis. These results support complexity and nonlinear dynamics measures of smooth pursuit as candidate markers for Parkinson's disease screening, pending validation in larger independent cohorts.

all_scored.title: Detecting Temporal Concepts in Video Transformers via a No-False-Positives Test
all_scored.summary: Video models have the architecture to support encoding temporal aspects of the input, i.e. concepts that require more than one frame to define, like object movement. However, because motion and appearance change are entangled, a feature that appears to encode temporal concepts like object movement may instead encode non-temporal concepts like spatial presence at different positions whose activations merely correlate with motion. To resolve this, we introduce the No-False-Positives (NFP) test, a statistical test with a formal guarantee of statistical specificity for identifying features encoding temporal concepts. Using specially designed stimuli, we apply this test to representations produced by VideoMAE, V-JEPA2, and TimeSformer, and observe that temporal features exist in each model. We validate the test first by showing it yields no temporal features for the DINOv2 image-encoder. Then, using a synthetic representation space, we show that detection rate increases with a direction's projection onto the temporal subspace, and that Sparse Autoencoder features test-flagged as temporal project much more of their norm onto the temporal subspace than unflagged features. Interventions on temporal SAE features yield mixed results across models, suggesting that intervening on temporal features may not outperform a non-temporal feature baseline.

all_scored.title: From Hype to ROI: An Economic Model for LLM Adoption in Information Systems and Security Operations
all_scored.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) promise significant efficiency gains across information-intensive operations by automating repetitive language-based tasks. However, adoption decisions remain largely opportunistic, as organizations struggle to move from pilots to sustainable industrialization. Without systematic economic frameworks, practitioners cannot assess whether LLM investments create value in a given context. This paper develops a general economic model to support informed LLM adoption decisions in operational information systems. Facing high uncertainty, we represent parameters as random variables centered on authoritative benchmarks, and evaluate the model by Monte Carlo simulation across pessimistic-to-optimistic assumptions on LLM efficiency. The ROI distributions show the probability of profitability and the Value at Risk for each configuration, together with a sensitivity analysis of its main drivers. As a first instantiation, we apply the model to Security Operations Centers (SOCs), mapping workflows onto established standards to identify tasks suited to LLM augmentation. The model balances productivity gains, driven by alert volume, analyst effort, and LLM efficiency, against operational costs, including inference, infrastructure, and error remediation, covering both cloud API and self-hosted deployments. Results show that adoption economics are context-dependent, and that automation is an exploitable lever, gated by accuracy, while the cost of errors and the model's price are secondary. Across the analyzed models and prices, most configurations are unprofitable, with profitability limited to high-accuracy, low-uncertainty deployments. The model gives organizations a quantitative basis for evidence-based adoption decisions, by locating the boundary between profit and loss, and the loss risked beyond it.

all_scored.title: Contract-Based Agentic Systems Engineering: Delegation as Quotient for Assured System Design
all_scored.summary: A component an agent builds from a prompt can satisfy it and still break the system it joins, because the prompt omits what its neighbours assume of it. The artifact to hand over is computed, not written. A SysML v2 requirement with assumed and required constraints is an assume/guarantee contract, so when a system requirement is decomposed over fixed neighbours, the open component's requirement is the contract quotient, the weakest sound one, and again a SysML v2 requirement. Its required constraints carry the neighbours' assumptions, which a requirement for the mission alone drops and unit tests with mocked neighbours cannot reach. Signal Temporal Logic is closed under the quotient. We build the requirements, with derivation, allocation, satisfaction and verification, as a SysML~v2 model and compute the quotient from it. A case study delegates the local controller of a simulated warehouse robot, whose route crosses a worker's path and ends at a dock, to one language model under the quotient requirement, a mission-only requirement and a natural-language task, and scores the deliveries on live episodes against the system requirement from ground truth.

all_scored.title: Information-Theoretic Scaling Laws for Generative Diffusion Training
all_scored.summary: Diffusion models trained on increasingly large datasets sampled from the same data distribution will converge to the same learned distribution. However, in practice, a model trained on finite data depends on the particular training dataset; this dependence is reflected in properties of the model's outputs, such as memorization and sample quality. To understand this dependence through an information-theoretic lens, we study \textit{model information}, a computationally tractable measure of how much samples from the trained model depend on the particular training dataset. We explore its scaling behavior as model size and training dataset size vary. Specifically, we uncover two qualitatively distinct scaling regimes: (1) a nonlinear model information regime marking the transition from pure memorization to imperfect generalization, and (2) a generalization regime characterized by linear scaling of the model information and progressively improved generalization and sample quality. We then posit an information-theoretically principled scaling law to quantify these two regimes, and show that this law yields induced scaling laws for memorization and sample quality. We finally demonstrate that these induced scaling laws extrapolate well outside the fit's domain. Our results demonstrate information-theoretic principles for memorization and sample quality scaling laws in diffusion models. Our code is publicly available on \href{https://github.com/DruvPai/diffusion_info_theory_scaling_law}{GitHub}.

all_scored.title: Gaussian Approximation for Composition and Subsampling of Differentially Private Algorithms
all_scored.summary: The privacy analysis of differentially private stochastic gradient descent (DP-SGD) relies on bounds for the composition of subsampled mechanisms. The privacy of such a composition is bounded by that of a pair of product distributions, whose privacy loss is a sum of independent terms and has been analyzed via a variety of notions and concentration results. Yet, existing closed-form bounds either lose a logarithmic factor or require restrictive conditions on the noise scale and delicate analysis of subsampling. Further, while it is well known that sums of independent random variables are approximately Gaussian, existing CLT-based techniques give an approximation with a large error in $δ$. We show that the privacy loss of this pair is approximately Gaussian as long as each step has a small privacy loss except with small probability. Specifically, its privacy loss distribution is close to a Gaussian with the same mean and variance, after truncating the rare large privacy losses. The closeness in both directions is up to a shift of $\varepsilon$ that grows only as $\ln(1/β)$ for an additive error $β$ in $δ$ and is a lower-order term in typical applications. In particular, the composition satisfies Gaussian differential privacy up to a lower-order shift of $\varepsilon$ and the additive error $β$. We also give a simple way to analyze the resulting variance-based bounds for subsampled mechanisms which relies on the $χ^2$ divergence of a single step. For the Gaussian mechanism at sampling rate $1/t$ and $t>\ln^{3}(1/δ)$, this gives the predicted rate for $σ\gtrsim\max\{1,\sqrt{\ln(1/δ)}/\ln(t)\}$, whereas the standard Rényi-divergence analyses need $σ\gtrsim\sqrt{t\ln(1/δ)}/\ln(t)$. We extend these results to random allocation (balls-and-bins sampling), and show that it explains the high accuracy of the connect-the-dots method.

all_scored.title: TempShap: When and How Much a Feature Matters in Time-Series Forecasting
all_scored.summary: Attribution for a time-series forecaster should answer two questions that a feature-level scalar cannot: when in the input window a feature acts, and how much its influence changes across the forecast horizon. Most existing Shapley explainers treat each feature as one player and therefore collapse both axes. We propose TempShap, a retrospective, loss-based Shapley framework whose players are the individual input cells $(t,i)$. Its attribution tensor yields temporal-localization and horizon-impact profiles. We validate these against planted temporal structures, a tractable exact cell game, and a closed-form attribution oracle for a real linear forecaster. Permutation sharing estimates the cell-level game at localized perturbation cost. Under redundant inputs, one-at-a-time scores under-credit substitutable information, whereas the signed Shapley decomposition preserves total value and yields more reliable held-out deletion rankings under mean masking. A planted counterexample isolates the redundancy mechanism. Experiments show a deletion-ranking advantage across Shapley estimators, forecasting benchmarks, and model families. TempShap therefore makes fine-grained Shapley attribution both practical and operationally useful.

all_scored.title: Active Reachability Learning for Humanoid Recoverability Monitoring
all_scored.summary: Deploying humanoid task policies requires reliable runtime monitors that anticipate unrecoverable falls in time to trigger a fallback. We formulate this task as learning the stochastic, finite-horizon recoverability envelope of a given fallback policy. Synthesizing this monitor is challenging: existing methods assume training data naturally covers the recoverability envelope, yet acquiring such data remains a major bottleneck for contact-rich systems. Consequently, they recover only a fraction of the true envelope, leaving them prone to optimistic hallucinations for out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs. We resolve this via a unified framework that iterates between value learning and active exploration. Data exploration is reframed as a reach-avoid problem, where an uncertainty-guided explorer systematically uncovers unseen states while avoiding confidently unrecoverable regions. This loop is further supported by a combined Temporal Difference and Monte Carlo objective for accurate in-distribution value prediction and reliable uncertainty estimation. By explicitly treating the remaining high-uncertainty regions as unrecoverable, the monitor mitigates optimistic OOD hallucinations. Evaluated on stochastic benchmarks and a 29-DoF Unitree G1 humanoid, our approach drastically improves monitor coverage and accuracy and successfully transfers zero-shot to real-world hardware.

all_scored.title: MLIPDiff: Guiding Denoising Diffusion Models for Structure-Based Drug Design via Machine-Learned Interatomic Potentials
all_scored.summary: Diffusion models have become a dominant approach to structure-based drug design. However, because they are trained primarily to fit reference structures, they often place ligands in physically implausible poses that clash with the protein. We introduce MLIPDiff, an inference-time guidance method that can be applied to pretrained diffusion models for ligand generation. The method uses physics-informed guidance from UMA (Universal Models for Atoms), a machine-learned interatomic potential (MLIP). The guidance combines four weighted energy terms (protein-ligand interaction, ligand strain, steric clash, and pocket anchoring) and uses the original model checkpoint without retraining. On CrossDocked2020, MLIPDiff completely eliminates protein-ligand collisions while preserving the ligand's local geometry, improving bond-length distributions and physical plausibility relative to the base model. Compared to models such as NucleusDiff that are specifically designed to reduce atomic clashes, MLIPDiff achieves clash-free structures without compromising local geometry. It maintains the base model's PoseBusters pass rate and attains the best median Vina Score, Vina Min, and Vina Dock, surpassing both the base model and NucleusDiff, with a median of 59.6\% of ligands per pocket binding more strongly than the reference. MLIPDiff thus addresses a limitation of prior methods by generating physically plausible structures with favorable predicted binding affinity using a single frozen model and no additional training.

all_scored.title: Exploring Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures for Self-Supervised Representation Learning of Powder X-ray Diffraction Patterns
all_scored.summary: Powder X-ray diffraction (XRD) is the primary high-throughput method for resolving crystal structures, a cornerstone of materials science. As high-throughput synthesis and self-driving laboratories advance, automated XRD pattern analysis has become vital for accelerating materials discovery. However, traditional matrix factorization methods fail when lattice variations cause non-linear peak shifts. At the same time, supervised learning approaches face a combinatorial explosion when handling multi-phase mixtures. To overcome these challenges, we adopt a self-supervised Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) to learn representation embeddings from 1D diffraction patterns. By optimizing a masked self-prediction loss directly within the latent space, the framework captures high-level crystallographic semantics. Downstream evaluations show that lightweight attentive probes trained on frozen JEPA representations achieve space group classification and lattice parameter estimation accuracy close to much larger supervised vision transformers. Furthermore, latent probing reveals that the learned representation space naturally organizes physical transformations, isolating smooth trajectories for peak broadening. Interestingly, decoding along latent paths between single-phase crystal representations yields realistic multi-phase mixture patterns, demonstrating an emergent continuous structure learned without explicit multi-phase supervision.

all_scored.title: Tree Depth and Sample-Quality-Associated Features: Two Hidden Factors in Boruta Selection for RNA-Seq Data Classification
all_scored.summary: Boruta is a widely used method for selecting gene panels from RNA sequencing data, and its most used implementation recommends Random Forest trees of depth 3 to 7, an untested setting. We tested whether this setting changes which genes are selected, using pan-cancer data from The Cancer Genome Atlas (10,469 tumors, 33 cancer types) and breast cancer PAM50 subtyping (981 tumors, 5 subtypes). A leakage-free protocol fitted every label-dependent step inside training folds, measured every effect against seed-to-seed variation, and held out a locked test set per task. In pan-cancer data, shallow trees changed the selection far more than a new seed did: the top-500 overlap with unlimited-depth selections was 0.37 at depth 5, against 0.84 to 0.93 between seeds at depth 5 or unlimited depth. Shallow trees confirmed 3.5 times fewer genes, missed markers of large classes and produced less accurate 50-gene panels (balanced accuracy 0.809 vs 0.889). The effect vanished once the cap reached about 60 to 75% of the depth that unrestricted trees grow to, set mainly by the number of classes, not sample size, and leaving depth uncapped cost no accuracy in either task. The effect replicated in a second cross-validation repeat and under permutation importance. About a third of pre-filtered candidates also tracked sample quality within class; a within-class filter removed them without loss of test accuracy (balanced accuracy 0.943 vs 0.942 with 1,000 genes). We recommend uncapped trees, or a cap chosen from the realized tree depth, and a within-class quality filter before Boruta.

all_scored.title: The Emergence and Sparsification of a Syntactic Circuit
all_scored.summary: To understand the emergence of grammatical behavior in language models, we track circuits for subject-verb number agreement in pythia-1b and ten seeds of pythia-410m across training. We find that subject-verb agreement is learned early, and is initially handled by a diffuse collection of neurons. However, after agreement behavior has stabilized, the mechanisms responsible for it continue to reorganize. The attention heads which mediate agreement often shift during training: in the case of pythia-1b, behavior is controlled by two heads early in training but by a third (different) head later. Furthermore, the circuit shrinks over training, with pythia-1b's final circuit being strikingly sparse. We take these results to be informative about how linguistic knowledge emerges and is represented in a language model.

all_scored.title: All-in-One: A Composable Attack on LLM Transformations
all_scored.summary: Quantization, pruning, and model merging are popular transformations applied to deployment-ready LLMs to improve efficiency and downstream performance. Recent work has shown that these transformations can introduce a security threat: an adversary can train a model that passes safety checks in its pre-transformed state, only turning malicious once it is transformed for deployment. However, prior attacks target one specific transformation (e.g., quantization) and generally rely on transformation-specific techniques, making them difficult to combine in practice. In this work, we introduce a simple, composable attack framework that targets multiple transformations simultaneously and triggers when any one of them is applied by a user. Our key insight is that the effect of each transformation can be approximated as a perturbation to the model weights, allowing us to jointly train the model with a benign loss on the original model and a malicious loss on each simulated transformed model. These perturbations are simple enough to simulate at every training iteration across diverse transformations, making them practically combinable within a single training objective, enabling a unified attack. Through extensive experiments across attack scenarios, model families, and a wide range of deployment-time model transformations, we show that our attack achieves high success rates. This demonstrates that model transformations may be utilized to trigger significantly different behavior from the original model and reinforces the associated security concerns by demonstrating that a single attack can jointly target diverse transformations.

all_scored.title: Individual Fairness via Local Predictive Consistency
all_scored.summary: Individual fairness in machine learning requires that similar individuals receive similar predictions. Most existing definitions are pairwise in nature, imposing a Lipschitz constraint that must hold either globally across all pairs of data instances or locally within specified neighborhoods. In practice, however, such pairwise constraints may be overly restrictive and may not directly identify which individuals receive locally inconsistent predictions. We study local predictive consistency as a node-level relaxation of pairwise individual fairness, where each prediction is compared with a similarity-weighted average of predictions in its local neighborhood. This yields an interpretable node-level fairness score and a corresponding regularized learning approach based on local residuals. Since graph-based individual fairness depends critically on the underlying similarity structure, we make the construction of the neighborhood graph explicit and discuss threshold selection through graph-coverage diagnostics. Our approach applies to binary classification, regression, and time-to-event prediction. We further compare this formulation with pairwise constraint-based approaches and analyze the resulting fairness--performance trade-offs.

all_scored.title: Sharp Bounds on Continuous Treatment Effects under Unobserved Confounding
all_scored.summary: We study partial identification of conditional treatment effects with a continuous treatment under unobserved confounding. We target the conditional average potential outcome (CAPO) E[Y_x|z] and the conditional average treatment effect (CATE) between two treatment levels. We assume a bounded outcome and Lipschitz continuity of the response functions and of the propensity scores given the latent confounder, and show that these conditions imply the smooth treatment response and smooth treatment selection conditions of Kim et al. (2018). The combined bound of Kim et al. uses only two reference points on the identified diagonal and is generally loose. Bounding through every diagonal reference point instead gives explicit bounds whose average is the sharp identified set of the CAPO at every treatment, inside or outside the observational support. Capping the difference between the upper and lower bounds gives sharp causal bounds on the CATE. These bounds are informative without monotonicity or overlap assumptions.

all_scored.title: GEMS-RAG: Graph-grounded Engineering Multimodal Standards Retrieval-Augmented Generation
all_scored.summary: Engineering standards are challenging knowledge sources for large language models (LLMs) because they are hierarchical, multimodal, and densely connected through figures, tables, cross-references, and normative rules. Existing retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) methods often rely on unstructured text retrieval and struggle with questions requiring joint reasoning over textual provisions, visual specifications, and document structure. We propose GEMS-RAG (Graph-grounded Engineering Multimodal Standards Retrieval-Augmented Generation), a framework for grounded reasoning over engineering standards. GEMS-RAG combines hierarchical parsing, fine-grained visual entity extraction, multimodal knowledge graph construction, and graph-grounded hybrid retrieval. Instead of treating figures as monolithic images, it decomposes them into meaningful visual entities linked to textual provisions, engineering concepts, and regulatory rules. During inference, dense, sparse, and visual retrieval are combined with graph expansion to identify relevant evidence across text, figures, and document structure. We evaluate GEMS-RAG on the Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices (MUTCD), a large engineering standard containing egulations, technical drawings, and standardized traffic-control devices. Results show that graph-grounded multimodal retrieval improves retrieval effectiveness and question-answering performance over text-only, multimodal, and graph-based RAG baselines. Beyond MUTCD, GEMS-RAG offers a general framework for reasoning over engineering codes, technical manuals, regulatory documents, and scientific standards in safety-critical applications.

all_scored.title: Neuromorphic Decision Dynamics for Deadlock-free Safe Navigation in Congested Environments
all_scored.summary: Safe navigation in congested environments requires both collision avoidance and coordinated passage. We introduce neuromorphic decision dynamics (NDD), a decentralized, event-based controller, that provides navigation in congested spaces with guarantees on safety, liveness, robustness, and scalability.
